summary: Arabic nouns have three cases, shown by the short vowel at the end of the word (iʿrāb, إِعْرَاب): nominative -u, accusative -a, genitive -i — with tanwīn when the noun is indefinite (-un, -an, -in). The nominative (الرَّفْع) is the subject form: the subject of a sentence and the predicate of a nominal sentence both take it — الْكِتَابُ هُنَا (the book is here), هٰذَا بَيْتٌ (this is a house). The accusative comes with objects (lesson 7) and after كَانَ / لَيْسَ, the genitive after prepositions and in “X of Y” (lesson 11). In everyday speech, and always at the end of a phrase (the pause form, الْوَقْف), the endings are mostly not pronounced: الْكِتَابُ is said al-kitāb — but careful MSA and this course write them.

blocks.caption: The indefinite accusative -an is written with an extra alif: بَيْتًا. Feminine nouns in ة take the endings on the ة: غُرْفَةٌ، غُرْفَةً، غُرْفَةٍ.

blocks.title: In this lesson everything is nominative.
blocks.text: In a sentence without a verb both parts are nominative: الْغُرْفَةُ هُنَا — هُنَا غُرْفَةٌ — هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ — الْمُعَلِّمُ هُنَا. You already know the other endings from كَانَ: هُوَ طَالِبٌ → كَانَ طَالِبًا.

blocks.title: The pause form.
blocks.text: At the end of an utterance the case vowel and the -n are dropped: الْبَابُ هُنَاكَ is said al-bābu hunāk; a final -an becomes -ā (شُكْرًا = šukrā / šukran). Dialects have lost the cases altogether, so you will hear al-bāb, bayt. Read the endings, but do not be surprised when people skip them.

blocks.title: Diptotes.
blocks.text: Some nouns (many broken plurals such as نَوَافِذُ، مَصَابِيحُ، حَقَائِبُ، أَصْدِقَاءُ) never take tanwīn and have only two endings when indefinite: -u, and -a for both accusative and genitive. With the article they behave normally: النَّوَافِذُ، النَّوَافِذَ، النَّوَافِذِ.

items: find who or what the sentence is about = subject
after كَانَ / لَيْسَ, a preposition or as an object → another case

blocks.text: How to find the subject: in a sentence without a verb it is usually the first noun or pronoun (الْكِتَابُ هُنَا) — unless an indefinite subject has been moved after the place (هُنَا كِتَابٌ: the subject is كِتَابٌ). In a verbal sentence it is the doer, often after the verb (كَانَ الْهَاتِفُ هُنَا).

askYourself: Who or what is the sentence about? That word is the subject → nominative (-u, -un).
Is there no verb? → the predicate (طَالِبٌ، مُعَلِّمَةٌ، كَأْسٌ) is nominative too.
Is there a كَانَ or لَيْسَ? → its predicate is accusative (-a, -an).
Does the noun have the article? → -u / -a / -i without -n; no article → -un / -an / -in (or a diptote).
Is the noun a diptote (نَوَافِذُ، حَقَائِبُ)? → no tanwīn.

traps: *الْبَيْتٌ: the article and tanwīn never go together — الْبَيْتُ or بَيْتٌ.
After كَانَ the predicate is not nominative: كَانَ طَالِبًا, not *كَانَ طَالِبٌ — but the subject of كَانَ stays nominative: كَانَ الْهَاتِفُ هُنَا.
The indefinite subject placed after هُنَا / هُنَاكَ is still the subject: هُنَا قَلَمٌ (nominative), not *هُنَا قَلَمًا.
Not hearing the endings in speech does not mean they are wrong in writing: write الْكِتَابُ even if you hear al-kitāb.

quiz.q: “The room is here” — which form of غُرْفَة?
“This is a book” — which form of كِتَاب?
quiz.why: The predicate of a sentence without a verb is nominative too: -un.

quiz.q: “I was a student” — which form of طَالِب?
quiz.why: The predicate of كَانَ is accusative.

quiz.q: Why do you often hear al-kitāb for الْكِتَابُ?
options: the pause form and the dialects drop the case vowel
quiz.answer: the pause form and the dialects drop the case vowel
quiz.why: At the end of an utterance (الْوَقْف) and in everyday speech the endings are left out; MSA writing keeps them.

seeAlso.note: German has four cases (Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ, Genitiv), carried mostly by the article (der / den / dem / des); Arabic has three, carried by the noun’s own ending.
Modern Hebrew has no cases — it lost the old Semitic case endings that Arabic keeps; only word order and prepositions (אֶת before a definite object) show the role.
Chinese has no cases at all: the place in the sentence shows who does what.
The accusative -a / -an of the direct object comes in lesson 7 (أَكَلْتُ الْخُبْزَ).

notes.text: Greek also puts both the subject and the predicate of a “be” sentence in the nominative (ο Γιάννης είναι δάσκαλος); Arabic does the same in a verbless sentence — but after كَانَ the predicate turns accusative.
Russian also changes the ending of the noun itself; Arabic has three cases instead of six, carried by one short vowel: -u, -a, -i.
Spanish nouns have no cases; in Arabic the last vowel shows the role: -u subject, -a object, -i after a preposition.
English shows case only in pronouns (I / me, he / him); every Arabic noun has three endings: الْبَيْتُ, الْبَيْتَ, الْبَيْتِ.
French nouns never change for case; Arabic nouns change their last vowel: -u, -a, -i.
Hindi nouns have a direct and an oblique form and take postpositions; Arabic has three case vowels on the noun and prepositions before it.
Persian nouns have no case endings (only -rā marks a definite object); Arabic nouns end in -u, -a or -i by their role.
Marathi marks roles with suffixes and postpositions on an oblique stem; Arabic with three case vowels at the end of the noun.
Turkish also marks case with endings; Arabic has only three, and marks the subject too (-u), where Turkish leaves it bare.
Japanese marks roles with particles after the noun (が, を, に); Arabic with the noun’s own last vowel (-u, -a, -i).
Korean particles (이 / 가, 을 / 를) do the job of the Arabic endings -u and -a.
Finnish has fifteen cases; Arabic has three and leaves place and direction to prepositions.
Hungarian has many cases and a bare nominative; Arabic has three and marks the nominative too (-u).
Swahili nouns have no case endings; in Arabic the end of the noun changes with its role.
Luganda nouns have no case endings; Arabic nouns change their last vowel with their role.
Vietnamese nouns never change; Arabic nouns change their last vowel with their role.
Inuktitut has many cases and marks the subject of a transitive verb differently from that of an intransitive one (ergative); Arabic marks every subject the same way, with -u.
